title: Fast and slow changes: why some happen in a second and some take years

summary.text: A sparkler burns out in less than a minute, but an iron gate takes months to rust. Both are chemical reactions: changes that make new substances. Some reactions are fast and some are slow. Heat, smaller pieces and a helper can make a reaction go faster. A helper that speeds up a reaction without being used up is called a catalyst. Hydrogen peroxide sits in its bottle for months, but next to raw potato it fizzes at once. The potato holds a catalyst called catalase, and so do your own blood and cells.
summary.art: On one side, a child holding a bright sparkler at night. On the other side, a rusty iron balcony grill. In the middle, a clear glass with white foam rising over grated potato.

intro.hook: A bottle of hydrogen peroxide can sit on a shelf for months and hardly change. Drop in a little raw potato, and it starts to foam within seconds. The potato is still there at the end. So what did the potato do?
intro.text: Every day you see changes that make new substances. A matchstick flares in one second. A dosa browns in two minutes. A banana goes spotty in a few days. A balcony grill rusts over many months. In this unit you time these changes, and find out what makes one fast and another slow. Then you test a helper hidden inside a potato.
intro.art: A row of pictures from fast to slow: a matchstick flaring, a dosa browning on a tava, a banana with brown spots, and a rusty iron hook, with a clock over each one.

outcomes: I can explain that a chemical reaction makes new substances, and give examples of fast and slow reactions at home.
I can put everyday changes in order from fastest to slowest, such as a sparkler, a dosa browning, a banana ripening and an iron gate rusting.
I can say that heat and smaller pieces usually make a reaction go faster, and explain why in terms of particles bumping into each other.
I can explain that a catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up, and show it with potato and hydrogen peroxide.
I can run a fair test with three cups, measure the foam, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that enzymes are catalysts made by living beings, and say how catalase helps a cell stay safe.
I can tell how Eduard Buchner showed in 1897 that juice squeezed from ground yeast, holding no whole cells, can still change sugar.

terms.meaning: A change in which substances turn into new substances. You usually cannot get the old substances back easily.
terms.example: When an iron nail rusts, the iron joins with oxygen and water to make rust, a new brown substance.
terms.art: An iron nail, shiny at one end and covered in orange-brown rust at the other.

terms.meaning: A reaction that is over in seconds or a few minutes.
terms.example: A sparkler burns from end to end in less than a minute, with sparks flying all the time.
terms.art: A sparkler fizzing with bright sparks in a dark sky.

terms.meaning: A reaction that takes hours, days, months or years.
terms.example: A silver anklet slowly turns dark over many months as the silver joins with tiny amounts of sulfur in the air.
terms.art: Two silver anklets side by side, one bright and new, one darkened.

terms.meaning: The tiny bits that every substance is made of. They are far too small to see, and they are always moving.
terms.example: In warm water the particles move faster than in cold water.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle showing tiny balls jiggling inside a drop of water.

terms.meaning: A substance that makes a reaction go faster and is not used up. It comes out of the reaction the same as it went in, so it can work again.
terms.example: Raw potato makes hydrogen peroxide break down fast. Strain the potato out and drop it into fresh peroxide, and it makes that foam too.
terms.art: Grated potato in a tea strainer being lowered into a fresh glass of liquid, with bubbles starting.

terms.meaning: A catalyst made by a living being. Every cell makes thousands of different enzymes.
terms.example: Your saliva has an enzyme that breaks starch into sugar. Chew plain rice for a long time and it starts to taste a little sweet.
terms.art: A child chewing, with a zoomed-in bubble showing long chains breaking into small sweet pieces.

terms.meaning: An enzyme that breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, very fast. Potatoes, yeast and your own blood all carry this enzyme.
terms.example: Grated raw potato in hydrogen peroxide is soon covered in white foam full of oxygen bubbles.
terms.art: A glass with a layer of grated potato at the bottom and a tower of white foam above it.

terms.meaning: A clear liquid that looks like water. On its own it slowly breaks down into water and oxygen over months. A weak kind is sold at chemists' shops.
terms.example: Its bottle is usually brown or white plastic and says 'store in a cool place', because light and heat speed up its breakdown.
terms.art: A small brown chemist's bottle with a label and a picture of the Sun crossed out.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air. Living beings use it to get energy from food, and fire needs it to burn.
terms.example: The bubbles in the potato foam are oxygen gas.
terms.art: Bubbles rising through a glass, with a small label saying oxygen.

terms.meaning: The outside of a thing, where it touches whatever is around it. Breaking a thing into small pieces gives it much more surface.
terms.example: Powdered eggshell has far more surface than one big piece of shell, so vinegar can touch more of it at once.
terms.art: One big piece of eggshell next to a heap of eggshell powder, with arrows showing liquid touching each grain.

explanations.definition: A chemical reaction is a change in which the particles of some substances rearrange to make new substances.
explanations.description: When ice melts, it is still water. That is a change of state, not a reaction. When a dosa browns, new substances with new smells and tastes are made. That is a chemical reaction. Signs of a reaction are a new colour, a new smell, bubbles of gas, light, or heat. Reactions happen everywhere: in the kitchen, on the balcony grill, and inside every cell of your body.
examples: Burning a matchstick makes ash, smoke and gases. You cannot turn them back into a matchstick.
Iron joins with oxygen and water to make rust.
Vinegar poured on eggshell makes bubbles of a new gas, carbon dioxide.
explanations.art: Two panels: an ice cube melting into water, labelled 'same substance', and a dosa browning on a tava, labelled 'new substances'.
explanations.context: This card is about what a chemical reaction is, so you can spot one.

explanations.concept: Some reactions are fast and some are slow
explanations.definition: The speed of a reaction is how much new substance it makes in a given time.
explanations.description: Reactions run at very different speeds. The powder in a cracker reacts in a tiny part of a second, so it bangs. A sparkler burns for less than a minute. A dosa browns in about two minutes. A banana skin goes from yellow to spotty in a few days. An iron gate rusts over months. A copper roof or a bronze statue turns green over many years. Scientists measure speed by how fast a new substance appears, or how fast an old one disappears. In your potato test, you measured it by how fast the foam rose.
examples: Fast: crackers, sparklers, a matchstick flaring, baking soda fizzing in lemon juice.
In between: a dosa browning, a papad roasting, milk turning brown when boiled down for payasam.
Slow: a banana ripening, an iron grill rusting, a silver anklet turning dark, a copper vessel going dull.
explanations.art: A long ribbon from left to right with pictures on it: a cracker, a sparkler, a dosa, a banana, a rusty gate and a green statue, with labels from 'a second' to 'years'.
explanations.context: This card is about how reactions can take a second or many years.

explanations.concept: Why heat and small pieces speed up a reaction
explanations.definition: Particles react only when they meet and bump into each other hard enough. Anything that makes them bump more often, or harder, makes the reaction faster.
explanations.description: For two substances to react, their particles must touch. In warm things the particles move faster, so they bump more often and harder. That is why food cooks on the stove and keeps for longer in the fridge. Breaking something into small pieces gives it much more surface, so more particles can meet at once. That is why eggshell powder fizzes in vinegar all at once, while a big piece fizzes slowly for hours. Rust is slow partly because the air touches only the outside of the iron, and partly because iron and oxygen react slowly at room warmth.
examples: Idli batter rises overnight in a warm Chennai kitchen. In a cold hill-town winter, such as Shillong or Ooty, it can take much longer.
Milk kept in the fridge stays fresh for longer than milk on the kitchen shelf.
A heap of fine sawdust can burn in a flash, but a thick log of the same wood burns slowly.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in picture of particles in a cold cup moving slowly with few bumps, and particles in a warm cup moving fast with many bumps marked by little stars.
explanations.context: This card explains why warmth and small pieces make reactions faster.

explanations.concept: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up
explanations.definition: A catalyst is a substance that makes a reaction go faster without being used up. It is the same at the end as at the start.
explanations.description: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen on its own, but very slowly. Raw potato holds a catalyst called catalase. Catalase holds a peroxide particle in just the right way, so it breaks apart easily, and then lets go of the water and oxygen. Then it is free to take the next one. One catalase can do this millions of times every second. That is why the foam rose so fast in your test. It is also why the same strained potato made fresh peroxide foam again. Boiled potato hardly worked, because heat changes the shape of catalase, and its shape is what lets it work.
examples: Catalase in raw potato and in yeast breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
A car's catalytic converter holds a little platinum and other metals. They help turn poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful ones.
Factories make fertiliser from the nitrogen in air, using iron as a catalyst.
explanations.art: A cartoon of a catalase shape like a cupped hand holding a small peroxide particle, then the particle breaking in two, then the hand empty and ready again.
explanations.context: This card explains what the potato did to the hydrogen peroxide in your test.

explanations.concept: Enzymes: how living beings make changes fast at body warmth
explanations.definition: An enzyme is a catalyst made by a living being. Most enzymes are proteins with a special folded shape.
explanations.description: A living being has a problem. They need thousands of reactions to happen fast: to break food down, to build new parts and to clean up harmful leftovers. But a cell cannot heat itself up like a stove. Enzymes solve this. Each one speeds up one kind of reaction at body warmth. Cells make a little hydrogen peroxide as they use oxygen, and peroxide can harm a cell. So cells, from potatoes and yeast to you, make catalase, which breaks peroxide down at once. Your saliva has another enzyme, amylase, which starts breaking starch into sugar while you chew.
examples: Amylase in your saliva turns some of the starch in rice into sugar as you chew.
Catalase in your blood breaks down hydrogen peroxide. That is why peroxide fizzes on a cut.
Enzymes from microbes turn sugar into gas in idli and dosa batter, which makes it rise.
explanations.art: A plant cell, a yeast cell and a human blood cell side by side, each with a little catalase shape inside breaking a peroxide particle.
explanations.context: This card is about the catalysts that living beings make, and why they need them.

explanations.concept: Were the first catalysts of life made of RNA?
explanations.description: Today most enzymes are proteins. But in 1982 Thomas Cech's team found that some RNA can act as a catalyst too. RNA is a substance that cells use to carry instructions. Some scientists think the very first living things used RNA both to carry instructions and as their catalysts, before protein enzymes existed. This is called the RNA world idea. It is an idea, not settled. Nobody knows yet how the first life began.
examples: Inside every cell, the machine that builds proteins, the ribosome, uses RNA to join the building blocks together.
Scientists have made new RNA catalysts in the lab.

perspectives.who: Scientists who support the RNA world idea
perspectives.explanation: RNA can both carry instructions and speed up reactions, so it could have done both jobs before proteins came along.
RNA is fragile and hard to make without help. Life may have started some other way, for example with simple reactions on minerals near hot springs on the sea floor.

explanations.art: A long wiggly RNA strand folded into a shape, holding two small pieces and joining them, in a dark early-Earth sea.
explanations.context: This card is about an open question: what the first catalysts of life were.

agreed.text: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up by it.
agreed.evidence: Chemists can weigh a catalyst before and after a reaction and find the same amount. You can see it at home: the same strained potato makes fresh peroxide foam again.

agreed.text: Most reactions go faster when things are warmer.
agreed.evidence: This has been measured for thousands of reactions. Cooks use it every day: food cooks on heat and keeps longer in the cold.

agreed.text: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces makes it react faster.
agreed.evidence: Powdered eggshell fizzes in vinegar far faster than a piece of the same weight. Fine flour dust in a mill can even catch fire in a flash, so mills must keep dust down.

agreed.text: Enzymes are catalysts made by living cells. Most are proteins, and their shape lets them work.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have seen the shapes of thousands of enzymes using X-rays and microscopes. Heat that changes the shape, like boiling, stops the enzyme working, as boiled potato showed.

challenging.claim: A catalyst gets used up, like fuel.
challenging.for: Many things in a reaction do get used up: the wax in a candle, the fuel in a stove.
challenging.against: Strain the potato out of foamy peroxide and drop it into fresh peroxide, and it foams again. Chemists weigh catalysts before and after and find the same amount. A catalyst can slowly wear out or get dirty, but the reaction does not use it up.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that a helper in a reaction must be used up.

challenging.claim: Fast reactions are dangerous and slow ones are safe.
challenging.for: Crackers and fires are fast and can hurt people.
challenging.against: Baking soda fizzing in lemon juice is fast and safe. Rust is slow, but it can weaken a bridge or a balcony grill until it breaks. Speed and danger are different things.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a fast reaction is always a dangerous one.

challenging.claim: Elizabeth Fulhame described catalysis about 40 years before it got its name.
challenging.for: In her 1794 book, Fulhame, a Scottish chemist, wrote that water helps some metal reactions happen and is made again at the end. That is the idea of a catalyst. The word 'catalysis' was made up by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1835.
challenging.against: Other historians say her idea was about water only, and was not yet the general idea of a catalyst that chemists use today.
challenging.context: This card is about who first saw the idea of a catalyst, and how much credit an early idea deserves.

big_questions.q: The peroxide in the plain cup was ready to break down all along, but it waited for months. What is a change doing while it waits?
big_questions.hint: Think about the particles. Are they still bumping? Why do so few bumps lead to a change?

big_questions.q: The potato helped the peroxide change, and came out the same. Did the potato take part in the change, or only watch it?
big_questions.hint: The catalase holds each peroxide particle while it breaks. Is holding taking part?

big_questions.q: Your body is warm, never as hot as a stove. How can it break down a whole meal in a few hours?
big_questions.hint: Think about the enzyme in your saliva, and the rice that turned sweet.

big_questions.q: Rust is slow for us. To a mayfly that lives for one day, would a sparkler seem slow? Are 'fast' and 'slow' in the change, or in the one who watches?
big_questions.hint: Compare how long the change takes with how long the watcher lives.

big_questions.q: People help each other do things faster without being used up, like a teacher who teaches many children. Is a teacher like a catalyst? In what ways not?
big_questions.hint: A catalyst comes out the same. Does a teacher come out the same after teaching?

story.title: Paati's Brown Bottle
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly on its own, catalase in raw potato and in blood breaks it down fast, cooking stops catalase working, and a sparkler and rust are both reactions with oxygen. Doctors now advise cleaning small cuts with clean running water, not peroxide.
text: It was the morning of Deepavali in Madurai, and the whole flat smelled of oil and sweets. Paati had been awake since four. Arjun, who was eight, had been awake since five, because he could not wait for the evening and the sparklers.

"Before any crackers, we clean," said Paati. She was his grandmother, and before she retired she had taught chemistry at a girls' school for thirty-one years. "Bring the first-aid box down from the shelf. We will throw away whatever is too old."
Arjun climbed on a chair to reach the box. As he jumped down, his knee hit the corner of the table. A thin red scrape appeared, and a drop of blood came up.
Paati washed the scrape under the tap with clean water for a long time. "Clean water is what doctors say is best for a small scrape," she said, and dabbed it dry with a fresh cloth.

Then she opened the first-aid box. Inside, behind the cotton and the plasters, was a small brown bottle. Paati held it up to the window. "Hydrogen peroxide," she read. "When I was a girl, my amma poured this on every cut. It fizzed white on the skin, and I thought the fizz was the germs running away."
"Was it?" asked Arjun.
"No," said Paati. "Tell me something first. This bottle has been on that shelf for many months. Look at it. Is it fizzing?"
Arjun looked. The liquid inside was still and clear, like water.
"So why did it fizz on your knee, and not in the bottle?"
Arjun thought. "Maybe my knee was warm?"

"A good guess. Warmth does speed things up. Let us test it." Paati went into the kitchen. She poured a little peroxide into two clear glasses. Into one she dropped a slice of raw potato from the vegetable basket. Into the other she dropped a piece of potato from last night's sambar, cooked soft.
Arjun leaned close. On the raw slice, tiny bubbles appeared, then more and more, until a white froth covered it. On the cooked piece, almost nothing happened.
"Both glasses are the same warmth," said Paati. "Both pieces are potato. So what is different?"
"One was cooked," said Arjun slowly. "The cooked one doesn't work. So there is something in raw potato that cooking spoils."

Paati smiled the smile she used to give her best students. "Its name is catalase. It is an enzyme, a helper that living cells make. Peroxide breaks into water and oxygen all by itself, but very slowly, a little every week. Catalase makes it happen at once. Those bubbles are oxygen."
"And on your knee, when you were small?"

"My blood has catalase too. So does yours. Your cells make a little peroxide every day as they use oxygen, and too much of it would harm them. So every cell keeps catalase ready, to break it down quickly." She lifted the raw slice out with a spoon and dropped it into a fresh glass of peroxide. It started to froth again.
"It's not used up!" said Arjun.
"No. A helper that speeds up a change and comes out the same is called a catalyst. Cooking changes its shape, and then it cannot hold the peroxide any more."

That evening, the balcony was crowded with cousins. Paati lit the first sparkler from a diya and gave it to Arjun, and held his wrist while it burned. White sparks sprayed out, and in less than a minute it was a black wire. Arjun dropped the wire into a bucket of water, as Paati had told him.
"That was fast," he said.

"Very fast," said Paati. She tapped the iron balcony grill. Orange-brown rust had crept along its bottom bar. "And this is the same kind of change. Iron is joining with oxygen from the air. But the grill has taken six monsoons to get this rusty."
Arjun looked from the black sparkler wire to the rusty grill to the dark sky full of crackers. "So everything is changing," he said. "Only some things are in a hurry."
"And some have a helper," said Paati, and lit him another sparkler.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the peroxide in the bottle was breaking down all the time, but so slowly that nothing showed. Catalase in raw potato, and in blood, is a catalyst. It makes the same change happen in seconds and is not used up, which is why the strained slice made fresh peroxide froth again. Cooking changes the shape of catalase, so the cooked potato hardly worked. Warmth was a fair guess, but both glasses were at the same warmth, so the test ruled it out.
ask: Why did the peroxide fizz on the raw potato but not in the bottle?
Arjun guessed his knee was warm. How did Paati's two glasses test his guess?
Why did Paati put the same raw slice into a fresh glass?
The sparkler and the grill both react with oxygen. Why is one so fast and the other so slow?
Arjun said, 'Everything is changing, only some things are in a hurry.' Can you think of something in your home that is changing too slowly to see?

experiments.title: The Potato and the Peroxide: what makes the foam?
experiments.question: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down very slowly on its own. Does raw potato make it break down faster? Does cooked potato? And is the potato used up?
experiments.predict: Look at the three cups: peroxide alone, peroxide with raw potato, and peroxide with boiled potato. Guess which cup will make the most foam, and which the least. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three cups get the same amount of peroxide, the same drop of soap and the same spoonful of potato. They stand side by side, so they are equally warm. Only one thing changes: no potato, raw potato or boiled potato. Measure every cup after the same time, 2 minutes.

materials.item: hydrogen peroxide, 3%, from a chemist's shop. If yours says 6% or '20 volume', mix it half and half with water.
a raw potato, peeled and grated, about 2 heaped teaspoons
a small piece of boiled potato, cooled and mashed, about 2 heaped teaspoons
3 clear glass tumblers or clear plastic cups, all the same size
dishwashing liquid, one drop for each cup
a measuring spoon or a tablespoon, a ruler and a tea strainer
3 paper labels and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up opens the bottle and pours the hydrogen peroxide. Use the 3% kind from a chemist's shop. If the label says 6% or '20 volume', mix it half and half with water first. Keep it away from eyes and mouth, and never drink it. If it splashes on skin, wash with plenty of water. Wash hands and cups afterwards, and put the bottle away where small children cannot reach it.

schedule.what: Guess, then set up three cups of peroxide. Add raw and boiled potato. Measure the foam. Strain the raw potato into fresh peroxide to see if it still works.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the three cups with their foam. Last, write three lines: what I think, what I saw, and why.

setup.art: Three clear tumblers in a row on a steel plate, each with two tablespoons of clear liquid and a label: 'Nothing', 'Raw potato', 'Boiled potato'.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the same peroxide into three labelled cups, and add one drop of soap to each.

setup.art: A hand tipping a spoonful of grated raw potato into the middle cup and a spoonful of mashed boiled potato into the third cup.
setup.caption: 2. Add raw potato to one cup and boiled potato to another. Add nothing to the first.

setup.art: The middle cup with a tall tower of white foam, the boiled-potato cup with a thin layer of bubbles, and the plain cup still clear, with a ruler held beside the middle cup.
setup.caption: 3. After 2 minutes, measure the foam in each cup with a ruler.

setup.art: A tea strainer holding grated potato over a sink, then the same potato dropped into a fresh cup, which begins to foam.
setup.caption: 4. Strain out the raw potato and drop it into fresh peroxide.

flow.do: 1. Grate about 2 heaped teaspoons of peeled raw potato. 2. Mash 2 heaped teaspoons of cold boiled potato. 3. Label three cups 'Nothing', 'Raw potato' and 'Boiled potato'.
flow.say: We are going to test a clear liquid called hydrogen peroxide. On its own it breaks down into water and oxygen, but very slowly. Let's see if potato changes that.
flow.kid: This clear liquid is hydrogen peroxide. It looks like water. Do not touch it or taste it. Help label three cups.
flow.parent: Grate the potato just before the test, because grated potato starts to change colour within a few minutes. Boiled potato from the day's cooking is fine if it has no salt or masala on it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Potato and Peroxide test. Here you get the potato and the cups ready.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three cups and the two kinds of potato. 2. Ask for a guess for each cup, and a reason. 3. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Which cup do you think will make the most foam? Which will make the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three cups. Which will foam most? Which least? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the raw potato cup will foam more?
good: Because raw potato is fresh and still has its juice.

ask.q: What do you think will happen in the cup with nothing?
good: Nothing, because there is nothing to make it change.
Maybe a little, because the liquid breaks down slowly on its own.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Any guess with a reason is a good guess.

flow.do: 1. Pour 2 tablespoons of peroxide into each cup. 2. Add one drop of dishwashing liquid to each. 3. At the same moment, tip the raw potato into its cup and the boiled potato into its cup. 4. Start a timer for 2 minutes.
flow.say: Now watch all three cups closely. The soap catches any gas as foam, so we can see it and measure it.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the liquid. Watch all three cups. What do you see?
flow.parent: In the raw potato cup, bubbles appear on the potato within seconds and white foam rises over the next minute, often 1 to 3 cm high. The boiled potato cup makes few or no bubbles. The plain cup stays clear. If the raw cup makes very little foam, the peroxide may be old. Try a new bottle.

flow.do: 1. After 2 minutes, hold a ruler beside each cup. 2. Measure from the top of the liquid to the top of the foam. 3. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Let's measure the foam in each cup. Hold the ruler straight up, next to the glass.
flow.kid: Hold the ruler next to each cup. How many millimetres of foam? Write it down.

check.q: The plain cup had no potato and made no foam. Why do we need that cup at all?
options: To show what peroxide does on its own, so we can compare
check.why: The plain cup shows what the peroxide does with no potato. Only by comparing with it can we say the potato made the difference. A cup like this is called a control.

flow.do: 1. Pour the raw potato cup through a tea strainer into the sink. 2. Rinse the potato in the strainer with a little water. 3. Put 2 tablespoons of fresh peroxide and a drop of soap in a clean cup. 4. Tip the strained potato in.
flow.say: Is the potato used up? Here is a test. We give the same potato some fresh peroxide. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Is the potato used up? Guess first. Then watch the fresh cup.
flow.parent: The fresh cup foams again, often almost as much as the first time. This shows the potato's helper was not used up. It may foam a little less each time, because some catalase washes away or wears out.

check.q: The same strained potato made fresh peroxide foam again. What does that show?
options: The potato's helper was not used up
Potato makes foam in any liquid
check.why: The potato's helper, catalase, came out of the first cup still able to work. A helper that speeds up a change and is not used up is called a catalyst. If you are not sure, try the strained potato in plain water with soap: it does not foam.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this. 'I think raw potato has something that makes peroxide break down fast. The raw cup made 25 mm of foam, the boiled cup 2 mm and the plain cup none. Cooking must spoil the helper.' Now read the catalyst card together.
flow.think: The peroxide in the plain cup was breaking down too, just too slowly to see. How could you find out?

experiments.title: Piece or Powder: which eggshell fizzes faster in vinegar?
experiments.question: Does the same eggshell react faster with vinegar as one big piece or as a fine powder?
experiments.predict: One glass gets a big piece of eggshell and the other gets the same amount crushed to powder. Which will fizz faster? Which will be finished first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use shell from the same egg, the same amount in each glass, the same vinegar, the same amount of it and the same place. Only one thing changes: one piece, or powder.

materials.item: the shell of one egg, rinsed and dried. If your family does not use eggs, use a clean broken seashell, or ask a neighbour for one shell.
white vinegar, the kind sold for cooking
2 clear glasses, the same size
a sheet of paper and a rolling pin or a steel tumbler, to crush the shell

experiments.safety: Vinegar stings in the eyes. If it splashes, rinse with water. Wash hands after handling raw eggshell.

schedule.what: Crush half the shell to powder. Put the piece and the powder in vinegar. Watch for 10 minutes.
Look at both glasses the next morning. Is the piece still there? Is it still fizzing?

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both glasses after 1 minute and the next morning.

setup.art: An eggshell broken into two halves on a steel plate, one half being folded in paper and crushed with a rolling pin.
setup.caption: 1. Break the shell in two. Crush one half to fine powder in a fold of paper.

setup.art: Two clear glasses of vinegar, one with a single curved piece of shell, one with white powder fizzing hard.
setup.caption: 2. Drop the piece in one glass and the powder in the other, at the same moment.

setup.art: The next morning: the powder glass is still and clear, the piece glass still has a few bubbles on a thinner, softer shell.
setup.caption: 3. Look again after 10 minutes and the next morning.

flow.do: 1. Break the shell into two halves that look the same size. 2. Fold one half in paper. 3. Crush it with a rolling pin until it is fine powder.
flow.say: We need the same amount of shell twice. One stays as a piece. The other becomes powder.
flow.kid: Crush one half of the shell into powder. Roll hard!
flow.parent: Peel off the thin skin inside the shell if it comes away easily. It does not matter much if some stays.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Piece or Powder test. You get two equal amounts of shell ready, one whole and one crushed.

flow.do: Ask for a guess about each glass, with a reason. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Eggshell and vinegar make bubbles of a gas called carbon dioxide. Which glass will fizz faster? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which will fizz faster, the piece or the powder? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the powder will be faster?
good: Because the vinegar can touch more of it.
Because small bits are easier to break.

flow.do: 1. Pour 3 tablespoons of vinegar into each glass. 2. Drop the piece into one and the powder into the other, at the same moment. 3. Watch for 10 minutes and write what you see at 1 minute and at 10 minutes.
flow.say: Drop them in together. Which glass fizzes more? Keep watching. Which one stops first?
flow.kid: Drop them in together. Watch both glasses. Which fizzes more?
flow.parent: The powder fizzes hard at once and may foam up. It is usually finished within a few minutes. The piece makes a steady stream of small bubbles that goes on for hours.

check.q: Why does the powder fizz so much faster than the piece?
options: The powder has much more surface, so the vinegar touches more shell at once
Powder is a different substance from shell
The vinegar in that glass is stronger
check.why: It is the same shell and the same vinegar. Crushing it gave the shell far more surface, so far more of it touched the vinegar at once. Picking 'different substance' is a fair thought, but powder is only shell in small pieces.

flow.do: Next morning: 1. Look at both glasses. 2. Lift the piece out with a spoon and feel it. 3. Say what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.say: Is the piece still fizzing? How does it feel now? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Look at both glasses. Touch the piece. Is it soft? What do you think happened?
flow.parent: The piece is often thinner and bendy, and may still have a few bubbles on it. The vinegar has been slowly reacting with it all night.

experiments.title: The Helper Hunt: which vegetables carry catalase?
experiments.question: Raw potato has the helper catalase. Which other raw vegetables and fruits make hydrogen peroxide foam, and which make the most?
experiments.predict: Choose four raw vegetables or fruits from the kitchen. Put them in order: which do you think will make the most foam, and which the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of peroxide, the same drop of soap and the same heaped teaspoon of each grated vegetable. Measure each cup after the same time, 2 minutes. Keep one cup with nothing as a control.

materials.item: hydrogen peroxide, 3%
four raw vegetables or fruits, for example potato, carrot, cucumber, ginger, radish, beetroot or apple
5 clear cups the same size, a grater, a teaspoon, a ruler and dishwashing liquid

experiments.safety: A grown-up opens the bottle and pours the hydrogen peroxide. Use the 3% kind from a chemist's shop. If the label says 6% or '20 volume', mix it half and half with water first. Keep it away from eyes and mouth, and never drink it. If it splashes on skin, wash with plenty of water. Wash hands and cups afterwards, and put the bottle away where small children cannot reach it. A grown-up does the grating.

schedule.what: Grate four vegetables. Put each in a cup of peroxide. Measure the foam and put them in order.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, then draw a bar for each vegetable to show its foam height.

setup.art: Four small heaps of grated vegetables on a steel plate: potato, carrot, cucumber and ginger, each next to a labelled clear cup.
setup.caption: 1. Grate a heaped teaspoon of each vegetable, and label one cup for each.

setup.art: Five cups in a row, each with clear liquid, and a hand tipping grated carrot into one.
setup.caption: 2. Add each vegetable to its cup of peroxide. Leave one cup with nothing.

setup.art: Five cups with foam of different heights, and a ruler held beside the tallest.
setup.caption: 3. After 2 minutes, measure the foam in each cup.

flow.do: 1. Choose four vegetables. 2. Ask your child to put them in order of how much foam they will make, with a reason.
flow.say: Potato has catalase. Do other vegetables have it too? Put these four in order, from most foam to least. Why?
flow.kid: Put the four vegetables in order. Most foam first. Why did you choose that order?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Helper Hunt. You test which kitchen vegetables carry the helper that breaks down hydrogen peroxide.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: Because it grows underground like potato.

flow.do: 1. Grate one heaped teaspoon of each vegetable. 2. Pour 2 tablespoons of peroxide and one drop of soap into each of the five cups. 3. Add each vegetable to its own cup. Leave one cup with nothing.
flow.say: Now each vegetable gets its own cup. One cup gets nothing, so we can compare.
flow.kid: A grown-up grates and pours. You tip each vegetable into its cup.

flow.do: After 2 minutes, measure the foam in each cup with a ruler, and write it down.
flow.say: Let's measure every cup. Which has the tallest foam?
flow.kid: Measure the foam in each cup. Write the numbers down.
flow.parent: Most raw plant parts make some foam, because most living cells carry catalase. How much differs from vegetable to vegetable, and even between two potatoes. Your results are your own. There is no wrong answer here, only what you measured.

flow.do: 1. Put the vegetables in order from the test. 2. Compare with the guess. 3. Ask: what do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.say: Was your order right? Which surprised you? Why do you think so many vegetables have catalase?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Which one surprised you? Why?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that many plants carry catalase, because their cells also make a little hydrogen peroxide and need to clear it away.

check.q: Most of the raw vegetables made some foam. What is the best reason?
options: Most living cells make catalase to break down peroxide
The soap made the foam by itself
check.why: Cells make a little hydrogen peroxide as they use oxygen, and too much can harm them. So most living cells keep catalase ready. The soap cannot be the reason, because the cup with nothing had soap too and stayed flat.

activities.title: A Few Seconds or a Season? Two changes side by side

materials.item: half a teaspoon of baking soda
half a lemon, or 2 tablespoons of vinegar
something rusty from the home: an old key, a nail, a hook, or the balcony grill
a steel plate and a clock or phone

schedule.what: Watch baking soda fizz in lemon juice, then look closely at rust. Guess how long each change took.

activities.record: Write how long you think each change took.

setup.art: A child squeezing lemon juice onto a heap of baking soda on a steel plate, with fizzing bubbles.
setup.caption: 1. Squeeze lemon juice on baking soda. Watch the fizz.

setup.art: A child looking closely at an orange-brown rusty iron hook on a balcony grill.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely at something rusty.

flow.do: 1. Put half a teaspoon of baking soda on the steel plate. 2. Squeeze lemon juice over it. 3. Count the seconds until the fizzing stops.
flow.say: Watch the baking soda when the juice touches it. Count how long the fizz lasts.
flow.kid: Squeeze the lemon on the baking soda. Count how long it fizzes.
flow.context: This is a short first look at a fast change and a slow change. Baking soda fizzes in lemon juice within seconds, while rust takes months.
flow.parent: The fizz is bubbles of a new gas, carbon dioxide. It lasts from a few seconds to about half a minute, then stops when one of the two is used up.

flow.do: Look closely at the rusty thing together. Touch the rust and look at the colour on your finger.
flow.say: The fizz and this rust are both chemical reactions. Each one made something new. How long do you think this rust took?
flow.kid: Look at the rust. Rub it with a finger. How long did it take to grow?

ask.q: How long do you think the rust took to grow?

flow.do: Ask the big question of the unit, and leave it open.
flow.say: One change took seconds. One took months. What do you think makes a change fast or slow?
flow.kid: One change took seconds. One took months. Why?
flow.parent: Don't answer yet. Write down your child's ideas. The experiments test them.

activities.title: The Change Ribbon: from fastest to slowest

materials.item: a long strip of paper, about 2 metres, or several sheets taped end to end
the 16 change cards from the Faster Wins game, or 16 slips of paper with the changes written on them
crayons and tape

schedule.what: Lay 16 changes along a paper ribbon from fastest to slowest. Check the times and move any that are in the wrong place.

activities.record: Draw the ribbon in your notebook, or stick it on the wall.

setup.art: A long paper ribbon on the floor marked 'a second', 'a minute', 'an hour', 'a day', 'a month', 'a year', 'many years'.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the ribbon from 'a second' to 'many years'.

setup.art: A child placing a card with a picture of a banana on the 'a few days' part of the ribbon.
setup.caption: 2. Place each change card where you think it belongs.

flow.do: Write these marks along the ribbon, spread out: a second, a minute, an hour, a day, a month, a year, many years.
flow.say: This ribbon is a clock for changes. Fast changes go at this end. Slow ones go at that end.
flow.kid: Write the marks on the ribbon. A second at one end. Many years at the other.
flow.context: This activity puts everyday chemical reactions in order of how long they take.

flow.do: Your child places each of the 16 change cards on the ribbon, saying why.
flow.say: Where does a dosa browning go? Where does a silver anklet turning dark go? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put each card on the ribbon. Say why you put it there.
flow.parent: Rough answers: cracker bang, less than a second. Match head flaring, about a second. Baking soda in lemon juice, a few seconds of fizz. Papad roasting, about 10 seconds. Sparkler, under a minute. Raw potato in hydrogen peroxide, about a minute. Dosa browning, about 2 minutes. Eggshell powder in vinegar, about 5 minutes. Idli batter rising, about 8 to 12 hours. Big eggshell piece going soft in vinegar, about a day. Turmeric fading in the sun, 2 to 3 days. Banana going spotty, 4 to 5 days. Iron grill rusting, months. Silver anklet darkening, months. Copper vessel going dull, months. Bronze statue turning green, many years.

flow.do: Read out the rough times. Move any card that is in the wrong place. Talk about the surprises.
flow.say: Which card moved the most? Which change surprised you? Rust and the sparkler both use oxygen from the air. Why is one so slow?
flow.kid: Which card moved most? Which one surprised you?

check.q: Where does the 'Idli batter rises' card go on the ribbon?
check.why: Idli batter takes about 8 to 12 hours to rise. That is more than an hour and less than a day.

activities.title: Small Elephant Toothpaste: yeast as a helper

materials.item: hydrogen peroxide, 3%
a packet of dry yeast, from a grocery or baking shop
warm water, 3 tablespoons
dishwashing liquid, a big squirt, and a few drops of food colour if you have them
an empty clear plastic bottle, about half a litre, standing in a tray or a big steel plate, and a funnel or a rolled sheet of paper

activities.safety: A grown-up opens the bottle and pours the hydrogen peroxide. Use the 3% kind from a chemist's shop. If the label says 6% or '20 volume', mix it half and half with water first. Keep it away from eyes and mouth, and never drink it. If it splashes on skin, wash with plenty of water. Wash hands and cups afterwards, and put the bottle away where small children cannot reach it. The foam is only soap, water, oxygen and yeast. Touch the foam only when a grown-up says so, and wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Mix yeast with warm water. Pour it into peroxide and soap in a bottle, and watch the foam rise out of the top.

activities.record: Draw the foam coming out of the bottle. Write what the yeast did.

setup.art: A clear plastic bottle standing in a steel tray, with a funnel in its neck and a grown-up pouring clear liquid in.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up pours peroxide and soap into a bottle standing in a tray.

setup.art: A child stirring a small cup of yeast in warm water with a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Mix the yeast with warm water for one minute.

setup.art: Thick white foam pouring out of the top of the bottle and spreading in the tray.
setup.caption: 3. Pour in the yeast and stand back.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bottle in the tray. 2. Pour in the peroxide. 3. Add a big squirt of dishwashing liquid and a few drops of food colour.
flow.say: We are making a foam so big it is called elephant toothpaste. Our helper this time is yeast.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the liquid into the bottle. You add the colour.
flow.context: This activity uses yeast, which carry catalase too, to break down hydrogen peroxide very fast.

flow.do: Mix one teaspoon of dry yeast with 3 tablespoons of warm water in a cup. Stir for one minute.
flow.say: Yeast are tiny living beings. Their cells carry catalase, the same helper as the potato. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Stir the yeast into warm water. Guess what will happen.

ask.q: What do you think the yeast will do?
good: Break the peroxide into water and oxygen.

flow.do: Pour the yeast mixture into the bottle quickly, and step back.
flow.say: Pour it in and step back. Feel the side of the bottle after a minute. Is it warm?
flow.kid: Pour in the yeast. Step back. Watch the foam come out!
flow.parent: With 3% peroxide the foam rises steadily out of the bottle neck for a minute or two. It will not be as huge as the videos, which use much stronger peroxide that is not safe at home. The bottle gets a little warm, because this reaction gives out heat.

check.q: Where did the gas in the foam come from?
options: The hydrogen peroxide broke down into water and oxygen
The yeast breathed the gas out
check.why: Catalase from the yeast broke the hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. The soap only trapped the oxygen as foam.

flow.do: Talk about what happened, then clean up with water.
flow.say: The potato and the yeast both had catalase. Why do you think such different living beings carry the same helper?
flow.kid: The potato and the yeast both had the helper. Why?
flow.parent: A good answer: both use oxygen, both make a little peroxide, and both need to break it down before it harms their cells.

activities.title: Chew and Wait: the helper in your mouth

materials.item: a spoonful of plain cooked rice, with no salt, or a small piece of plain chapati
a clock or phone to time 2 minutes

schedule.what: Chew plain rice slowly for 2 minutes and notice if the taste changes.

activities.record: Write how the rice tasted at the start and after 2 minutes.

setup.art: A child holding a spoon of plain white rice, with a clock beside the plate.
setup.caption: 1. Take a spoonful of plain rice. Taste it.

setup.art: The child chewing slowly with eyes closed, and a zoomed-in bubble showing long starch chains breaking into small sugar pieces.
setup.caption: 2. Chew slowly for 2 minutes without swallowing.

flow.do: Your child takes a spoonful of plain rice and notices the taste.
flow.say: Taste the rice. Is it sweet, salty or plain?
flow.kid: Taste the rice. Is it sweet? Salty? Plain?
flow.context: This activity shows an enzyme in your own saliva at work.

flow.do: Your child chews slowly for 2 minutes, without swallowing, and says if the taste changes.
flow.say: Keep chewing slowly. Tell me if the taste changes.
flow.kid: Chew slowly. Don't swallow yet. Does the taste change?
flow.parent: Many children notice a faint sweetness after a minute or two. Some do not, and that is fine. The change is small, and taste differs from person to person.

flow.do: Explain what was happening, after your child has said what they noticed.
flow.say: Your saliva has an enzyme called amylase. It is a catalyst. It breaks the starch in rice into sugar. Why do you think your body starts this in the mouth?
flow.kid: Your saliva has a helper. It breaks starch into sugar. Why start in the mouth?

check.q: Why does chewed rice start to taste sweet?
options: An enzyme in saliva breaks starch into sugar
check.why: Amylase in saliva is a catalyst. It breaks the long starch chains in rice into small sugars, which taste sweet.

activities.title: Be the Particles: why warmth speeds things up

materials.item: a clear space on the floor, and 6 cushions or pillows
a phone or clock to time 30 seconds

schedule.what: Act out cold and warm particles. Count how many times you bump into a cushion in 30 seconds.

activities.record: Write the two counts: cold and warm.

setup.art: A child walking very slowly among cushions scattered on a floor, labelled 'cold'.
setup.caption: 1. Cold: walk slowly among the cushions for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The same child moving quickly among the cushions, bumping into them, labelled 'warm'.
setup.caption: 2. Warm: move fast among the cushions for 30 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Scatter the cushions. 2. Your child walks very slowly among them for 30 seconds, with eyes half closed. 3. Count every bump.
flow.say: You are a particle in cold water. Move slowly. Every time you bump a cushion, that is a chance to react.
flow.kid: You are a cold particle. Walk slowly. Count your bumps.
flow.context: This act-out shows why particles react faster when they are warm.

flow.do: Your child moves quickly among the cushions for 30 seconds. Count the bumps again.
flow.say: Now you are a particle in warm water. Move faster. Count your bumps.
flow.kid: Now you are warm. Move fast. Count your bumps.
flow.parent: Keep it safe: fast walking, not running, on a clear floor.

flow.do: Compare the two counts and talk about them.
flow.say: Which time had more bumps? Were the bumps harder? Why do you think food cooks faster when it is hot?
flow.kid: Which time had more bumps? Why does hot food cook faster?

check.q: Why do most reactions go faster when things are warm?
options: Warm particles move faster, so they bump more often and harder
check.why: Warm particles move faster. They meet more often and bump harder, so more bumps lead to a change. Heat is not a substance, so it is not a catalyst.

projects.title: Sun or Shade: a 3-day turmeric watch

materials.item: half a teaspoon of turmeric powder and a little water
2 strips of white paper or old white cotton cloth, about 5 cm by 15 cm
a sunny windowsill and a dark drawer
a piece of cardboard to cover half of one strip, and tape

schedule.what: Paint two strips with turmeric. Put one on a sunny windowsill, with half of it covered by cardboard. Put the other in a dark drawer.
Look at both strips. Lift the cardboard and compare the covered and uncovered halves.
Put all three parts side by side. Draw them and say what sunlight did.

projects.record: Each day, draw the strips and colour them as bright as they look. Write which part is palest.

setup.art: Two strips of white paper painted bright yellow with turmeric paste, drying on newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Paint two strips with turmeric paste.

setup.art: One strip taped to a sunny window with cardboard over half of it, and a drawer with the other strip inside.
setup.caption: 2. One strip in the sun, half covered. The other in a dark drawer.

setup.art: Three yellow pieces side by side: a pale sunny half, a bright covered half and a bright strip from the drawer.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3, compare all the parts.

flow.do: 1. Mix turmeric with a few drops of water into a paste. 2. Paint both strips evenly. 3. Let them dry. 4. Tape one to a sunny window and cover half of it with cardboard. 5. Put the other in a dark drawer.
flow.say: Turmeric's yellow colour slowly breaks down in light. Washermen have long dried turmeric stains in the sun to fade them. Will the sun make it faster? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Paint the strips yellow. Put one in the sun, half covered. Put one in a drawer. Guess what will happen.
flow.context: This project tests whether light speeds up a slow change: the fading of turmeric's yellow colour.

ask.q: Why did we cover half of the sunny strip?
good: So we can compare sun and no sun on the same strip.
Because it is a fair test.

flow.parent: Turmeric stains clothes and hands, so wear old clothes and work on newspaper.

flow.do: Look at both strips. Lift the cardboard gently and look under it, then put it back.
flow.say: Has anything changed since yesterday? Which part looks palest?
flow.kid: Look at your strips. Which part is palest?
flow.parent: In strong sun the uncovered half often looks paler after one day. In cloudy weather it can take longer, so keep going for another day or two.

flow.do: 1. Take everything down. 2. Lay the sunny half, the covered half and the drawer strip side by side. 3. Draw them. 4. Say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.say: Which part faded most? What does that tell us about light and this change?
flow.kid: Lay them side by side. Which faded most? Why?
flow.parent: The uncovered sunny part should be palest. The covered half and the drawer strip stay bright yellow. Light gives the colour particles energy to break apart, so light can speed up a reaction, just as heat can.

check.q: The sunny half faded but the covered half stayed bright. What made the difference?
check.why: Both halves had the same air and the same paper. Only the light was different. So light sped up the fading.

challenges.title: The Foam Tower: make the most foam in one minute
challenges.problem: You have one tablespoon of potato and 2 tablespoons of hydrogen peroxide. Find a way to make the tallest foam tower within one minute.
constraints: You may use only one heaped tablespoon of raw potato.
You may use only 2 tablespoons of 3% peroxide and one drop of soap.
Measure the foam with a ruler after exactly one minute.
materials: a grater, a knife for a grown-up, a mortar and pestle or a steel tumbler for crushing
clear cups, dishwashing liquid, a ruler and a timer
general: Grate the potato finely instead of cutting it into one cube, so more surface touches the peroxide.
Crush the grated potato in a mortar to break open more cells.
Use a tall, narrow glass so the same foam rises higher.
creative: Warm the cup a little by standing it in a bowl of warm tap water, not hot, before adding the potato.
Try mixing the potato with the peroxide using a spoon for a few seconds.
Cut a fresh potato and grate it just before you start, so the catalase has had no time to change.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way. Write down your plan, test it, and measure. Then change one thing and test again.
challenges.safety: A grown-up opens the bottle and pours the hydrogen peroxide. Use the 3% kind from a chemist's shop. If the label says 6% or '20 volume', mix it half and half with water first. Keep it away from eyes and mouth, and never drink it. If it splashes on skin, wash with plenty of water. Wash hands and cups afterwards, and put the bottle away where small children cannot reach it.

setup.art: A cube of potato, a heap of grated potato and a mortar with crushed potato, side by side on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Choose how to prepare your potato.

setup.art: Two tall narrow glasses with foam towers of different heights, and a ruler between them.
setup.caption: 2. Test it and measure the foam after one minute.

flow.do: Read the problem together and look at the materials.
flow.say: Engineers make reactions go the speed they need. How could we make our potato work faster?
flow.kid: How can you make the most foam? Think of three ideas.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Foam Tower challenge. You use what you know about speeding up reactions.

flow.do: Draw three ideas before building.
flow.say: Draw your three ideas. Which do you think will work best? Why?
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. Which is best? Why?

flow.do: 1. Try the best idea. 2. Measure the foam after one minute. 3. Change one thing and try again.
flow.say: Measure after one minute exactly. Then change just one thing and test again.
flow.kid: Try your best idea. Measure the foam. Change one thing. Try again.

flow.do: Compare results and explain them.
flow.say: Which idea made the tallest tower? Why do you think it worked?
flow.kid: Which idea won? Why do you think it worked?

check.q: Meena, a girl in Class 3, grated her potato very finely and got more foam than her friend, who used one cube. Why?
options: Fine grating gave more surface, so more catalase touched the peroxide
Grated potato is a different vegetable
check.why: Grating breaks the potato into many small pieces with far more surface, and opens more cells. More catalase meets the peroxide at once, so the foam rises faster.

challenges.title: Keep It Bright: protect turmeric yellow from the sun
challenges.problem: Turmeric yellow fades in sunlight. Design a cover that keeps a turmeric-painted card bright yellow on a sunny windowsill for 2 days.
constraints: The card must stay on the sunny windowsill.
You must be able to see the card through or around your cover, or lift the cover to check.
materials: foil, coloured plastic, butter paper, cloth, cardboard
general: Cover the card with cardboard, which lets no light through.
Wrap it in aluminium foil, which reflects light away.
Keep it in a closed steel box on the windowsill.
creative: Try a see-through cover of coloured plastic, and test whether some colours protect better than others.
Make a tiny curtain that you open only to look.
Cover half of a card with foil and half with cloth, and see which half stays brighter.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own cover. Leave one card uncovered to compare. Check after two days. Which cover kept the yellow brightest?

setup.art: Two turmeric-yellow cards on a sunny windowsill, one under a little tent of foil, one uncovered.
setup.caption: 1. Put a covered card and an uncovered card side by side in the sun.

setup.art: After two days, the uncovered card pale and the covered card still bright yellow.
setup.caption: 2. After two days, compare the two cards.

flow.do: Read the problem together.
flow.say: Sunlight speeds up the fading of turmeric yellow. How could we slow it down?
flow.kid: Light fades turmeric. How can you keep it bright?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep It Bright challenge. You use what you found in the turmeric watch to slow a change down.

flow.do: Draw and build a cover. Paint two cards with turmeric.
flow.say: Draw your cover first. Why do you think it will work?
flow.kid: Draw your cover. Build it. Paint two cards yellow.

flow.do: Put both cards on the sunny windowsill, one covered and one not.
flow.say: Why do we need the uncovered card too?
flow.kid: Put both cards in the sun. One covered. One not.

flow.do: After two days, compare the cards and explain.
flow.say: Which card is brighter? Why did your cover work, or not work?
flow.kid: Which card is brighter? Why?

check.q: A cover of thick cardboard kept the card bright. Why?
options: It stopped the light that speeds up the fading
check.why: Cardboard blocks light. Without light, the colour breaks down much more slowly.

games.title: Faster Wins: a card game of fast and slow changes
games.context: This is a card game. Each card names a chemical change from home. Two cards are turned over, and players guess which change is faster.

printables.title: 16 change cards to cut out (the time is on the back)

items.f: Baking soda fizzes in lemon juice
A papad roasts on a flame
A sparkler burns from end to end
Raw potato makes hydrogen peroxide foam
A dosa browns on the tava
Eggshell powder stops fizzing in vinegar
A big eggshell piece goes soft in vinegar

A copper pot goes dull and dark

rules: Shuffle the 16 cards and put them in a pile with the words facing up. The times are on the backs.
Turn over the top two cards and lay them side by side. Do not look at the backs.
Each player says which change is faster, and why.
Flip both cards to read the times. Everyone who was right gets a point.
If both cards say the same time, everyone gets a point.
The first player to 6 points wins. If the pile runs out first, the player with the most points wins, and a tie is a shared win.
Playing alone? Lay all 16 cards in a line from fastest to slowest, then flip them to check. Count how many are in the right place.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and read the rules together.
flow.say: Each card is a change that makes a new substance. We guess which of two is faster.
flow.kid: Each card is a change. Guess which of two is faster.
flow.context: This is the start of the Faster Wins card game.

flow.do: Play until someone has 6 points. After each round, ask why.
flow.say: Why do you think the dosa is faster than the idli batter? Is heat helping?
flow.kid: Pick the faster change. Say why. Flip to check.
flow.parent: When a heated change beats an unheated one, point out the heat. When a powder beats a piece, point out the surface.

flow.do: End with one question.
flow.say: Which two cards were hardest to tell apart? Why?
flow.kid: Which two cards were hardest? Why?

rules: Two people can play: one is the catalyst and the other is the walker. With more people, one is the catalyst and all the others are walkers. Someone also times with a phone.
Put the 6 particle cards (3 A and 3 B) on the floor in different corners of the room, face up. Clear a joined pile space on a table or a mat.

Round 1, no catalyst: a walker carries one card at a time. To join a pair, a walker stands on one foot, holds an A and a B together and counts slowly to 20. If the other foot touches the floor, start the count again. Put the pair in the joined pile. Time how many seconds it takes until all 3 pairs have joined, or stop at 120 seconds and count the pairs.
Put all 6 cards back in their corners.

Round 2, with the catalyst: walkers carry one card at a time to the catalyst in the middle. The catalyst holds an A and a B together for a count of three and puts the pair in the joined pile. Time how long it takes for all 3 pairs to join.
Compare the two times. Then check: has the catalyst changed, or is she or he still standing in the middle, ready to help again?

setup.caption: 1. Round 1: join a pair the hard way, on one foot, counting to 20.

setup.art: A girl in the middle of the room holding an A card and a B card together for a count of three, with a child waiting beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Round 2: the catalyst joins the pair quickly and stays in the middle.

flow.do: Cut out the 7 cards and read them. Choose who is the catalyst. Put the particle cards in the corners.
flow.say: Two particles, A and B, must join to make something new. Joining is hard on their own. Then a catalyst helps.
flow.kid: Choose the catalyst. Put the particle cards in the corners.
flow.context: This is the start of Catalyst Tag, a game that shows how a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

flow.do: Play Round 1 with no catalyst. Time how long until all 3 pairs have joined.
flow.say: Go! Join the hard way. How many seconds until all three pairs are joined?
flow.kid: Join each pair on one foot, counting to 20. It is slow!

flow.do: Put the cards back. Play Round 2 with the catalyst. Time it again.
flow.say: Now the catalyst helps. How long does it take this time?
flow.kid: Carry an A and a B to the catalyst. Go!

flow.do: Compare the two times and talk.
flow.say: Which round was faster? Did the catalyst join any pair and sit down? What does that tell us?
flow.kid: Which round was faster? Is the catalyst still standing in the middle?

check.q: At the end of Round 2, the catalyst was still standing in the middle, ready to help again. What does that show about a real catalyst?
options: It is not used up by the reaction
check.why: The catalyst helped every pair and joined none of them, so it was free to help again. A real catalyst works the same way: it speeds up a reaction and comes out the same.
