quiz.p: Which of these is a chemical reaction?
opts: A dosa browning on the tava
quiz.why: Browning makes new substances with new smells and tastes. Melting, dissolving and breaking do not make new substances.
A sparkler takes under a minute, a papad seconds and a banana a few days. Rust takes months.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3 in Chennai, puts grated raw potato in hydrogen peroxide. White foam rises. What is the gas in the foam?
quiz.why: Catalase in the potato breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. The soap traps the oxygen as foam.

quiz.p: Kavya strains the same potato out and drops it into fresh peroxide. It foams again. What does this show?
opts: The potato's helper is not used up
The new peroxide is a different liquid
Potato makes foam in any liquid
The soap did all the work
quiz.why: The catalase came out of the first cup still able to work. That is what makes it a catalyst. Picking 'soap' means forgetting the plain cup, which had soap and stayed flat.

quiz.p: Why did boiled potato make little or no foam?
opts: Cooking changed the shape of the catalase, so it stopped working
Boiled potato is too soft to sink
Boiling took out all the water
quiz.why: Catalase works because of its shape. Boiling changes that shape, and then it cannot hold the peroxide. The boiled potato had cooled, so warmth was not the reason.

quiz.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Mysuru, drops a piece of eggshell into one glass of vinegar and the same amount of eggshell powder into another. Which fizzes faster?
quiz.why: Powder has much more surface, so more of the shell touches the vinegar at once.

quiz.p: Why does milk stay fresh longer in the fridge?
opts: In the cold, the changes that spoil milk go more slowly
quiz.why: Cold particles move slowly and bump less, so the changes that spoil milk go more slowly.

opts: A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up
A substance that always stops reactions
Any substance that gets used up in a reaction
quiz.why: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and comes out the same at the end.

quiz.p: An enzyme is a catalyst made by…
quiz.why: Enzymes are catalysts made by living cells, such as the catalase in potato and the amylase in your saliva.

quiz.p: In 1897 Eduard Buchner's team ground up yeast cells and squeezed out the juice. The juice held no whole yeast cells. What happened when he added sugar?
opts: The juice still changed the sugar, making gas bubbles
quiz.why: The juice still turned sugar into gas and alcohol. It showed that the changes are done by enzymes, which still work outside the cell.

quiz.p: Divya, a girl in Kochi, says: 'Rust is slow, so it is never a problem.' What is wrong with her idea?
opts: Over months and years, rust can weaken iron until it breaks
quiz.why: Slow does not mean harmless. Rust slowly eats into iron grills, gates and bridges, which is why they are painted.

worksheets.title: Fast, Slow and the Potato Helper (core)

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Kolkata, writes a list of changes in his home. Sort them: fast (seconds or minutes) or slow (hours or longer).
items.a: see items
items.why: The match, papad and sparkler take seconds. Rust, banana spots and darkening silver take days or months. A strong answer also says what new substance each change makes, such as rust or ash.

items.p: A catalyst is used up in the reaction it speeds up.
items.why: False. A catalyst comes out the same at the end. The strained potato made fresh peroxide foam again.

items.p: In the potato test, which cup was the control, the cup we compare the others with?
items.why: The cup with no potato shows what the peroxide does on its own. Comparing with it shows what the potato changed.

items.p: When things get warmer, their particles move ____ and bump into each other more often.
items.why: More bumps, and harder ones, mean a reaction can go faster.

items.p: Draw the three cups from the potato test after 2 minutes: nothing, raw potato and boiled potato. Show the foam in each.
items.a: Tall foam over the raw potato, little or no foam over the boiled potato, and a clear cup with nothing.
items.why: A strong drawing shows clear differences in foam height and labels each cup.
items.art: Three empty cup outlines in a row.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a change that makes new substances
speeds up a reaction and is not used up
a catalyst made by a living being
the enzyme that breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen
the gas in the potato foam
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit.

items.p: The plain cup of peroxide stayed clear. The raw potato cup foamed. Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
items.a: I think raw potato has a helper that breaks peroxide down fast. I saw tall foam in the raw cup and none in the plain cup. The helper is catalase, a catalyst.
items.why: A strong answer has a claim, evidence with a measurement, and a reason.

items.p: Put these changes in order, from fastest to slowest.
items.why: A match flares in a second, a dosa browns in minutes, batter rises overnight and rust takes months.

items.p: Why does a dosa brown in minutes on a hot tava, but raw batter does not brown on the kitchen shelf?
opts: Heat makes the particles bump faster and harder, so the browning reaction speeds up
The tava is a catalyst that gets used up
Batter on the shelf has no particles
items.why: Heat speeds up the browning reaction. The tava is not used up, and it is the heat, not the iron, that does the work here.

items.p: Rust and a burning sparkler both use oxygen from the air.
items.why: True. Both are reactions with oxygen. One is very slow and one is very fast.

items.p: Label the picture of the potato test: hydrogen peroxide, grated raw potato, foam, oxygen bubbles.
items.why: A strong answer puts each label in the right place and says that the bubbles hold oxygen.
items.art: A clear cup with liquid, grated potato at the bottom and foam on top, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Small pieces react faster than one big piece because they have more ____.
items.why: More surface means more of the substance touches the other substance at once.

items.p: Revathi and her brother Arun, in Madurai, look at the foamy potato cup.

views.says: The potato made the oxygen. It's coming out of the potato.
The oxygen came from the peroxide. The potato just helped.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what happened when the same potato went into fresh peroxide. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Arun, because the same potato made fresh peroxide foam again, so the oxygen came from the peroxide each time. Revathi has something right: the bubbles do appear on the potato, because that is where the catalase is.
items.why: Both children saw something real. Bubbles form on the potato, but the potato is not used up, so the oxygen must come from the peroxide.

items.p: Name one fast change and one slow change you have seen at home this week. Say what new substance each one made.
items.a: For example: a papad roasting made brown, crisp new substances in seconds. Our balcony grill is slowly making rust.
items.why: A strong answer names real changes and the new substance each makes.

items.p: Why do we use the same amount of peroxide in every cup?
opts: So only one thing changes, and the test is fair
items.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Then any difference must come from that one thing.

items.p: The peroxide bottle says 'store in a cool, dark place'. Using what you learned, explain why.
items.a: Heat and light both speed up the breakdown of peroxide into water and oxygen. In a cool, dark place it lasts much longer.
items.why: A strong answer names both heat and light, and links them to the speed of the breakdown.

items.p: Nandini, a girl in Bengaluru, wants her potato to make foam faster. Which change will help most?
opts: Grate it finely instead of using one cube
Put the cup in the fridge
items.why: Grating gives more surface, so more catalase meets the peroxide. Boiling stops the catalase and the fridge slows it down.

items.p: Two scientists talk about a car's catalytic converter, which helps change poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful ones.

views.says: It is wonderful. The metal inside is not used up, so it keeps cleaning the exhaust for years.
It helps, but it still lets out carbon dioxide, and the metals in it, like platinum, must be dug out of mines.

items.ask: Which view matters more to you? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other scientist has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and fairly says what the other side has right. For example: the catalyst is not used up, which is good, but it does not stop all harm.
items.why: Both views are true. A catalyst can make a reaction cleaner, but it does not remove every cost.

items.p: Draw particles in a cold cup and in a warm cup. Show how fast they move and how often they bump.
items.a: Few, slow arrows in the cold cup. Many, long arrows and many bumps in the warm cup.
items.why: A strong drawing shows faster movement and more bumps in the warm cup.
items.art: Two empty cup outlines labelled cold and warm.

items.p: Powdered eggshell and a piece of eggshell make the same total amount of gas, if they weigh the same and there is enough vinegar.
items.why: True. The amount of shell is the same, so the total gas is the same. The powder only makes it faster.

items.p: In the Helper Hunt, most raw vegetables made some foam. What is the best explanation?
opts: All vegetables have soap in them
items.why: Cells make a little peroxide as they use oxygen, so most cells carry catalase to break it down.

items.p: Put the steps of the potato test in order.
items: Pour the same peroxide into three cups
Guess which cup will foam most, and why
a: Guess which cup will foam most, and why
Pour the same peroxide into three cups
items.why: First guess, then set up, then add, then measure.

items.p: A family in Shillong says their idli batter takes much longer to rise in winter than in summer. Explain why.
items.a: In winter the kitchen is colder. The microbes and their enzymes work more slowly in the cold, so the batter rises more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer links cold to slower reactions, and mentions the microbes or enzymes.

items.p: The enzyme in saliva that breaks starch into sugar is called ____.
items.why: Amylase starts breaking down starch in your mouth.

items.p: Why did the strained potato foam a little less the second time?
opts: Some catalase washed away or wore out
The potato became a different vegetable
The fresh peroxide was the wrong colour
items.why: A catalyst is not used up by the reaction, but some can be lost when you rinse it, and enzymes slowly wear out.

items.p: On a picture of a rusty balcony grill, label: iron, rust, where the air touches, where rain collects.
a: where the air touches (all the outside)
items.why: Rust grows where iron meets air and water, most of all where water sits.
items.art: A balcony grill with orange patches on its bottom bar and four blank label lines.

items.p: A boy in your class, Arjun, says, 'Heat is a catalyst.' Is he right? Explain.
items.a: No. Heat speeds up reactions, but it is not a substance. A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up.
items.why: A strong answer separates heat, which is energy, from a catalyst, which is a substance.

items.p: Match each helper to what it speeds up.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Catalase and amylase are catalysts. Heat and light also speed up reactions, but they are not substances, so they are not catalysts.

items.p: Our bodies need enzymes because a body cannot heat itself up like a stove to make reactions fast.
items.why: True. Enzymes make reactions fast at body warmth, which is far cooler than a stove.

items.p: Draw the Catalyst Tag game: two particles joining with the help of the catalyst, then the catalyst free again.
items.a: Three panels: catalyst holding two particles' hands, the pair joined, the catalyst walking away alone.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the catalyst at the start and at the end, unchanged.
items.art: Three empty boxes in a row.

items.p: A bottle of peroxide breaks down slowly on its own, but there is a reason most cells cannot wait for that. Explain why living cells need catalase.
items.a: Cells make a little peroxide as they use oxygen. Peroxide harms cells. On its own it breaks down too slowly, so cells use catalase to break it down at once.
items.why: A strong answer names the problem first, then how catalase solves it.

items.p: In the 1800s, Louis Pasteur said that turning sugar into alcohol needs living yeast. In 1897, Eduard Buchner showed that yeast juice, which held no whole cells, could do it too.

views.says: Only living yeast can change sugar. I have never seen it happen without them.
Here is juice that holds no whole yeast cells. This juice changed the sugar anyway.

items.ask: Who do you think had the better evidence? Then say what Pasteur had right.
items.a: Buchner had the better evidence, because his test showed the change without whole cells. Pasteur had right that the substances doing the work come from living yeast.
items.why: Both were partly right. Enzymes are made by living cells, but they can still work outside them.

items.p: Sneha, a girl in Pune, wants to know whether warmth makes potato catalase work faster. Which test is fair?
opts: Two cups with the same peroxide and potato, one in cool water and one in warm water
One cup of warm peroxide with potato and one cup of cold peroxide with carrot
One cup in the sun and one in the shade with different amounts of potato
items.why: Only the warmth changes. The other tests change two things at once.

items.p: Iron grills rust faster in Chennai, near the sea, than in dry Jaipur. Suggest why.
items.a: Rust needs water as well as oxygen. In Chennai the air near the sea is damp and salty, so more water touches the iron and rust grows faster.
items.why: A strong answer names water as something rust needs and links more water to faster rusting.

items.p: Draw a picture that shows why a fine flour dust can burn in a flash but a heap of flour cannot.
items.a: Dust spread out in the air, with air around every grain, next to a heap where only the top grains touch the air.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that in the dust every grain touches air, so more surface reacts at once.

items.p: A cook in Kochi grates a coconut before adding it to the curry, instead of dropping in a big piece. Using what you know about surface, explain why the grated coconut gives its taste faster.
items.a: Grating breaks the coconut into many tiny pieces. This gives it much more surface, so more of it touches the hot curry at once and its taste spreads faster.
items.why: A strong answer uses the word surface and links more surface to a faster change.

items.p: A catalyst can make a reaction happen that would never happen at all on its own.
items.why: False. A catalyst speeds up a reaction that can already happen, often far too slowly to notice. Peroxide breaks down on its own too, just very slowly.

items.p: Why do people paint balcony grills?
opts: The paint stops air and water touching the iron, so it rusts much more slowly
items.why: Rust needs iron to touch air and water. Paint covers the iron and slows rusting down.

items.p: Some scientists think the first living beings used RNA as their catalysts. Explain what a catalyst would do for an early living being.
items.a: It would make the reactions the living being needed happen fast enough, without being used up.
items.why: A strong answer links catalysts to speed and says that a catalyst is not used up.

items.p: Put the steps of Buchner's 1897 test in order.
items: He added sugar to the juice
Yeast cells were ground with fine sand
The ground yeast was squeezed to get juice
a: Yeast cells were ground with fine sand
The ground yeast was squeezed to get juice
He added sugar to the juice
items.why: Grind, squeeze, add sugar, then see the gas.

items.p: On the drawing of the eggshell test, label: piece, powder, vinegar, bubbles of carbon dioxide.
items.why: A strong answer puts each label in place and names the gas.
items.art: Two glasses side by side, one with a shell piece and few bubbles, one with powder and many bubbles.

items.p: Match each way of changing a reaction to an example.
pairs: a dosa browning on a hot tava
turmeric staying bright in a drawer
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each example shows one thing that changes how fast a reaction goes.

items.p: One catalase can break down millions of peroxide particles every second. What does this tell you about why only a little potato is needed?
opts: Each catalase works again and again, so a little goes a long way
items.why: A catalyst is not used up, so a small amount can change a large amount of peroxide.

items.p: Slow reactions are always harmless.
items.why: False. Rust is slow, but over years it can weaken iron grills, gates and bridges.

items.p: Invent a catalyst game of your own for a friend. Draw how it shows that the helper is not used up.
items.a: Any clear game drawing in which a helper player helps others join or change and stays free at the end.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the helper unchanged at the end.

applications: Cooks use heat to speed up cooking, and fridges to slow down spoiling.
A car's catalytic converter uses metals such as platinum to turn poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful ones.
Fertiliser factories use iron as a catalyst to make ammonia from the nitrogen in air.
Washing powders contain enzymes that break down food and other stains in cool water.
Paint and oil on iron grills, gates and bridges slow down rusting.
Medicines are kept in cool, dark places, so the slow reactions that spoil them go even slower.
In 2018, Frances Arnold shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for ways of making new enzymes that do useful jobs.

open_questions.q: What were the first catalysts of life?

open_questions.q: Can we design new catalysts that turn carbon dioxide from the air back into useful fuels?
open_questions.why_open: Many teams are trying. Some lab catalysts work, but none yet is cheap and strong enough to use on a large scale.

maths.problem: In the potato test, the raw potato cup had 24 mm of foam and the boiled potato cup had 3 mm. How many times as much foam did the raw potato make?
maths.explain: The raw cup had 24 mm and the boiled cup had 3 mm. 24 divided by 3 is 8. So the raw potato made 8 times as much foam. Check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 24.
maths.context: This is about the potato test, where you measured the foam on three cups of hydrogen peroxide after 2 minutes. These are made-up example results.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one result by another tells us how many times stronger the raw potato's helper was.

maths.problem: A sparkler burns for 40 seconds. A dosa takes 2 minutes to brown. How many sparklers, one after another, would burn while one dosa browns?
maths.explain: 2 minutes is 120 seconds. 120 divided by 40 is 3. So 3 sparklers burn in the time one dosa browns.
maths.context: This is about the Change Ribbon, where you put changes in order from fast to slow.
maths.why_maths: Changing minutes into seconds lets us compare the speed of two changes in the same unit.

maths.problem: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, measured foam in the Helper Hunt: potato 20 mm, carrot 12 mm, cucumber 6 mm, ginger 15 mm. Put them in order from most to least. How much more foam did potato make than cucumber?
maths.answer: Potato, ginger, carrot, cucumber. Potato made 14 mm more than cucumber.
maths.explain: 20 is the biggest, then 15, then 12, then 6. 20 minus 6 is 14. These are made-up example results, and your own may be in a different order.
maths.context: This is about the Helper Hunt, where you tested which raw vegetables make hydrogen peroxide foam.
maths.why_maths: Putting numbers in order shows at a glance which vegetable's helper worked fastest.

maths.problem: In the turmeric watch, Lakshmi, a girl in Mysuru, gave each part a brightness score from 10 (bright) to 0 (white). Day 1: sunny half 10, covered half 10. Day 3: sunny half 4, covered half 9. Which part changed more, and by how much?
maths.answer: The sunny half changed by 6 points, the covered half by 1 point. The sunny half changed 5 points more.
maths.explain: Sunny: 10 minus 4 is 6. Covered: 10 minus 9 is 1. 6 minus 1 is 5. These are made-up example scores.
maths.context: This is about the 3-day turmeric watch, where one strip was in the sun with half of it covered.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the start from the end shows how much each part changed, so we can compare them fairly.

maths.problem: Iron grills in a flat need painting every 3 years to stop rust. How many times will they be painted in 12 years?
maths.explain: 12 divided by 3 is 4. So the grills are painted 4 times in 12 years.
maths.context: This is about rust, a slow reaction that paint slows down even more. The 3 years is a made-up example.
maths.why_maths: Dividing tells us how often a slow change must be dealt with over a long time.

roots.context: We have timed fast and slow changes, and watched a potato make peroxide foam without being used up. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The peroxide in your plain cup stayed clear. Beside raw potato, the same peroxide foamed within a minute. The strained potato then made fresh peroxide foam too. So how fast a change happens can depend on a helper that is not used up.
deep_truth.habit: We usually think the only things that take part in a change are the ones that get used up and turn into something new. The potato took part, came out the same, and could do it again. We also call things like the peroxide 'stable', when they are changing all the time, only slowly.
deep_truth.evidence: In the potato test, the plain cup made no foam, raw potato made tall foam and boiled potato made almost none. The same strained raw potato made fresh peroxide foam again.

three.who_am_i: Your blood and every cell in you carry catalase. Thousands of enzymes in you speed up the changes that keep you alive, at body warmth.
three.what_is_life: A living being cannot cook their food on a stove inside them. So every living being, from yeast to a potato to you, makes enzymes to make their changes fast.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything around you is changing, some things in a second and some over many years. Iron grills, silver anklets and even rocks are changing now, only slowly.

roots.thread: A bottle of peroxide looks still, but it is breaking down a little all the time. Every substance carries changes it is ready for, most of them too slow to see. It lets a change that was already possible happen now, and then it is free again. One small helper can change millions of particles.

teachings.teaching: On those who step into the same rivers, different and different waters flow.
teachings.link: The river looks the same from day to day, but its water is always new. A grill or an anklet also looks the same, but it is always slowly changing.

teachings.teaching: All made things do not last. When one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering.
teachings.link: Rust, fading colours and darkening silver show that made things slowly change. Speed is the only difference between a sparkler and a rusting gate.

teachings.teaching: With the best leaders, when the work is done, the people all say: we did it ourselves.
teachings.link: A catalyst helps a change happen and then steps away unchanged. The new substance is made from the peroxide alone, not from the helper.

science.text: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up. Enzymes are the catalysts of living cells.
Exactly how every enzyme achieves its speed is still being studied.

other_view.view: A catalyst is simply a substance that offers an easier path for a reaction. It is a useful tool, and reading lessons about leaders or helpers into it says more about people than about chemistry.

practice.title: Watch a slow change
practice.say: Let's find something in our home that is changing slowly. It could be the grill, a plant, or a banana. Now let's look at it in silence for one minute. It is changing right now, but too slowly for us to see. Then let's breathe slowly five times. Inside you, enzymes are speeding up thousands of changes with every breath.
practice.kid: Find something that changes slowly. Look at it for one minute. It is changing now. Breathe slowly five times. Your enzymes are busy too.

ask: The peroxide was changing all along, too slowly to see. What else around you might be changing that you can't see?
The potato helped and came out the same. Is a helper part of the change, or outside it?
If a change took a million years, would anyone ever notice it was a change?

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people used yeast to make bread rise and to turn fruit juice into wine. But what was the yeast doing? In the 1800s, the great French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that yeast are living beings. He thought that changing sugar needed whole living yeast cells, and could not happen without them. In 1897 in Germany, Eduard Buchner tested this. His brother Hans and Hans's assistant Martin Hahn had ground yeast with fine sand and pressed the paste hard, to get a juice that held no whole yeast cells. To keep the juice from spoiling, they added a lot of sugar, the way people keep fruit in jam. Soon the juice began to bubble. It was turning the sugar into gas and alcohol, just as living yeast does. Pasteur's idea was wrong. The work was done by substances that the yeast cells make, and these still work outside the cell. These substances are enzymes, the catalysts of living things. Buchner won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1907.
how_we_found_out.who: Eduard Buchner, a German chemist, with his brother Hans Buchner and Martin Hahn
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Louis Pasteur and many others thought that changing sugar into alcohol needed whole living yeast cells. Buchner's yeast juice, which held no whole cells, changed sugar too, which showed that enzymes made by the cells do the work.

playtest: Every experiment and activity was walked through on paper against its materials list, not tried in a kitchen. The potato test uses 3% hydrogen peroxide. Many Indian chemists sell 6% ('20 volume'), so the steps say to mix it half and half with water. Raw grated potato gives clear foam within a minute with a drop of dishwashing liquid, and the raw and boiled cups get the same amount of potato. Boiled potato gives little or none. Old peroxide may give weak foam, so the step says to try a new bottle. The strained potato usually foams again, a little less. The first activity uses baking soda and lemon, so the core path needs no flame. The eggshell test gives a vegetarian alternative, a broken seashell. The yeast foam is much smaller than online videos, which use strong peroxide, and the step says so. Turmeric fades fastest in strong sun, so the project says to keep going a day or two longer in cloudy weather. The rice-chewing activity may not taste sweet to every child, and the step says that is fine. Faster Wins works alone or with two. Catalyst Race works with two people: a catalyst and a walker.
